strengths: Identifies a significant and critical flaw in the widely used CrowdAI Mapping Challenge dataset, exposing that ~90% of training samples are duplicates and that 93% of validation images leak into the training set.
Provides an important cautionary message for researchers working on polygonal building footprint extraction in remote sensing imagery.
The perceptual hashing and discrete rotation/flip search strategy is computationally efficient, lightweight, and easy to reproduce.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The proposed pipeline simply applies standard DCT-based perceptual hashing (Algorithm 1 is vanilla pHash) combined with standard discrete rotations and flips. There is no novel algorithmic or methodological contribution to computer vision.

Lack of quantitative re-evaluation and benchmark experiments: While the paper claims to potentially invalidate recent state-of-the-art methods due to severe overfitting, it does not re-train or benchmark any models (such as PolyWorld, HiSup, PolyMapper) on the de-duplicated dataset. The claim relies solely on a few qualitative visualization examples in Figure 2 without any quantitative evidence.

Narrow scope: The analysis is restricted entirely to a single benchmark (CrowdAI). Evaluating data leakage and duplication across multiple popular aerial/remote-sensing or general vision benchmarks would provide substantially broader impact.

Incomplete presentation and formatting flaws: The manuscript contains placeholder text/missing URLs (e.g., at the end of the Abstract and in bullet 2 of Section 1), citation errors (e.g., Figure 2 cites PolyWorld as [12], which corresponds to Li et al., 2019, instead of [24]), and the main text spans roughly four pages, leaving substantial room for thorough empirical investigation.

strengths: Important empirical finding: The paper reveals a critical flaw in the widely used CrowdAI Mapping Challenge benchmark, uncovering that ~90% of the training images are duplicates/augmented duplicates and ~93% of the validation images leak into the training split.

Clear cautionary value for the community: Highlighting data leakage in popular benchmarks is vital to prevent researchers from drawing flawed conclusions regarding model generalization and overfitting.
weaknesses: Near-zero methodological novelty: The proposed 'drop-in pipeline' (Algorithm 1) is simply standard discrete cosine transform (DCT) perceptual hashing (pHash) paired with basic dihedral group augmentations (flips and 90-degree rotations). The paper presents standard off-the-shelf techniques without any new algorithmic or theoretical formulation.

Lack of quantitative downstream experiments: Despite claiming that prior state-of-the-art methods are potentially invalidated, the authors do not retrain any existing models (e.g., PolyWorld, HiSup, PolyBuilding) on the deduplicated dataset. The paper provides no quantitative benchmarking (e.g., changes in IoU, mAP, or boundary metrics before and after deduplication) to measure the true extent of performance degradation or metric inflation, relying entirely on five anecdotal visual crops in Figure 2.

Narrow scope: Despite the title promising a study on 'Large Scale Image Datasets', the empirical investigation is strictly confined to a single dataset (CrowdAI). No other benchmarks (e.g., SpaceNet, INRIA, COCO, ImageNet) are analyzed to demonstrate generalizability.

Incomplete and unpolished manuscript: The paper has notable placeholders (e.g., empty URLs on pages 1 and 2), erroneous citations (Figure 2 cites PolyWorld as [12], which points to a different paper by Li et al., rather than [24]), and very thin content (the core text spans only roughly 3.5 pages, padded out with sparsely laid-out tables and figures).

strengths: Identifies a critical data hygiene issue in the CrowdAI Mapping Challenge benchmark, revealing that approximately 90% of training samples are duplicates and ~93% of the official validation set leaks into the training set.
Provides a valuable cautionary finding for the remote sensing and building footprint extraction communities, highlighting why reported performance in prior works may be artificially inflated.
weaknesses: Very limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed pipeline is merely a standard, off-the-shelf perceptual hashing (DCT-based pHash) combined with simple discrete rotation and flip augmentations.

Lack of quantitative re-benchmarking: Although the manuscript claims prior state-of-the-art methods are invalidated by overfitting, it does not re-train or quantitatively evaluate any existing baseline (e.g., PolyWorld, HiSup) on the clean deduplicated split to measure the actual performance degradation.

Incomplete manuscript and formatting defects: There are missing URLs / placeholder text left unfilled (e.g., 'publicly available at' at the ends of Section 1 and Section 2), incorrect citation mapping (e.g., citing PolyWorld as [12] instead of [24] in Section 4 and Figure 2), and the main text spans only about 4 pages.
Narrow empirical scope: The analysis is restricted exclusively to a single dataset (CrowdAI), lacking broader evaluation or insights across other satellite or computer vision benchmarks.

strengths: Important empirical finding for the geospatial community: The discovery of severe duplicate contamination (~90% internal duplicates) and massive train-test/validation data leakage (>93%) in the widely used AICrowd Mapping Challenge benchmark is an eye-opening and impactful revelation. Many recent building extraction papers (e.g., PolyWorld, HiSup, Frame Field Learning) rely heavily on this benchmark.

Convincing demonstration of leakage impact: The supplementary experiment (Table 5) testing a pretrained HiSup model on seen versus unseen test splits clearly demonstrates performance inflation (dropping from 79.7 AP on seen images to 65.4 AP on unseen images), confirming that models memorized leaked training samples.

Comprehensive baseline audit: The paper evaluates multiple prominent datasets (INRIA Aerial, SpaceNet 2, and AICrowd) and accurately distinguishes genuine duplicates from false positives caused by low-contrast/no-data tiles.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The proposed pipeline simply applies standard discrete cosine transform (DCT) based perceptual hashing (pHash) with brute-force 90-degree rotations and flips. The paper does not propose a novel deduplication algorithm, representation learning strategy, or automated spatial leakage framework.

Lack of model retraining experiments: While the authors evaluate an existing checkpoint on the partitioned seen vs. unseen test subsets, they do not retrain models on the pruned/deduplicated training split (which shrank from ~280k to ~15k images). Demonstrating the downstream training efficiency, final model generalization, and establishing a corrected benchmark leaderboard would significantly elevate the contribution.

Neglect of geospatial spatial autocorrelation / spatial leakage: In remote sensing datasets, data leakage frequently occurs through spatially contiguous or overlapping tiling, even when tiles are not exact duplicates. The paper only investigates exact and rotated image duplicates, missing the broader geospatial challenge of spatial buffer leakage.
Incomplete text and formatting: On page 1 (Abstract and Introduction), the code repository link is left blank ("Our code is available at ").

strengths: Identifies a severe, critical issue in the widely used AICrowd Mapping Challenge benchmark, demonstrating that over 90% of validation and test images are leaked copies or augmented versions of training images.

Provides convincing empirical evidence (e.g., Table 5 in the supplementary material and qualitative predictions in Figure 3) showing that models memorized annotation errors and suffered notable performance drops (14.3 AP drop) on truly unseen test samples.
The analysis serves as an important cautionary tale for the geospatial and building footprint extraction community, which has relied heavily on AICrowd for benchmarking.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The proposed deduplication pipeline is simply off-the-shelf perceptual hashing (DCT-based pHash) evaluated under 8 dihedral geometric transformations (rotations and flips) with a Hamming distance threshold of 0. There is no novel methodology or algorithmic contribution presented.

Lack of geospatial-aware overlap analysis: Remote sensing datasets primarily suffer from data leakage due to overlapping spatial bounding boxes / geographic coordinates (e.g., sliding window tiling with small strides). A rigid image-space pHash with Hamming distance 0 completely fails to detect spatial overlap with translations, sub-pixel shifts, or different cropping boundaries. Incorporating spatial metadata / coordinate polygon intersections is standard and necessary for geospatial audit.

Limited experimental depth: The authors evaluate only one pre-trained model (HiSup) on the partitioned seen/unseen test splits, and do not retrain models from scratch on the deduplicated training set to examine how deduplication affects final convergence, representation learning, or relative model rankings.
Incomplete manuscript details: The abstract abruptly cuts off with 'Our code is available at ' without providing a link or repository information.

strengths: Important empirical finding: The paper reveals critical dataset flaws in the widely used AICrowd Mapping Challenge dataset, documenting that ~90% of training images have identical/augmented duplicates and ~93% of validation/test images leak into the training set.

Impact demonstration on downstream models: The authors illustrate how models trained on this contaminated benchmark (such as PolyWorld and HiSup) reproduce annotation errors (Figure 3) and experience notable drops in average precision (AP drops from 79.7 to 65.4) when evaluated strictly on unseen data (Table 5 in the supplementary).
Clear writing and motivation regarding dataset hygiene and benchmark integrity in remote sensing and computer vision.
weaknesses: Minimal methodological and technical novelty: The proposed deduplication pipeline consists entirely of standard Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT)-based perceptual hashing (pHash) applied to images augmented with trivial 90-degree rotations and reflections. There is no new algorithm, feature representation, or indexing methodology proposed.

Limited robustness beyond exact/grid-aligned transforms: The method relies entirely on explicit enumeration of 90-degree rotations and flips. It cannot handle continuous affine transformations, arbitrary crops, non-aligned overlapping bounding boxes, scaling, or near-duplicate variations commonly addressed in the copy detection and retrieval literature (e.g., DISC benchmarks).

High false-positive rate on low-texture imagery: As acknowledged in the paper and shown in Figures 7 and 8, the standard 64-bit DCT pHash collides frequently on uninformative or low-contrast patches (such as bodies of water, open fields, or nodata borders). The pipeline does not incorporate semantic verification or feature filtering to automatically distinguish true duplicates from untextured background tiles.

Lack of extensive re-benchmarking: Although the audit highlights the severity of the AICrowd dataset issues, the paper does not systematically retrain and re-benchmark competing state-of-the-art polygonization/segmentation methods on a properly cleansed, deduplicated split to show how method rankings and architectural choices are affected.
Incomplete submission details: The abstract ends abruptly with an incomplete sentence ('Our code is available at ').
